subject: Accounting
title: What Are Internal Controls?
description: A 60-second lesson on What Are Internal Controls?.

hook.text: A cashier can process refunds and pocket the cash. Without controls, nobody would ever know.

buildup.text: Internal controls are policies and procedures that safeguard assets and ensure accurate records.

discovery.text: They include approval processes, access restrictions, physical locks, and automated system checks.

twist.text: Good controls don't eliminate fraud—but they make it much harder and easier to detect.

climax.text: After Sarbanes-Oxley, public companies must document and test internal controls every year.

punchline.text: Controls don't assume honesty. They enforce it.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of internal controls?
options: To safeguard assets and ensure accurate records

details.summary: Internal controls are the policies, procedures, and systems a company implements to ensure financial reporting accuracy, comply with laws, prevent fraud, and protect assets — from segregation of duties to approval workflows.
details.whyItMatters: Strong internal controls are a company's first line of defense against errors and fraud. Auditors evaluate these controls to determine how much additional testing is needed on financial statements.
takeaways: Internal controls include segregation of duties, approval authorization, physical safeguards, and reconciliations
Strong controls reduce the risk of errors and fraud reaching the financial statements
Auditors test control effectiveness — stronger controls mean less detailed substantive testing is needed

faq.question: What are the main types of internal controls?
faq.answer: Preventive controls stop errors before they happen (approval limits, segregation of duties). Detective controls find errors after they occur (reconciliations, exception reports). Examples include dual signatures on large payments, bank reconciliations, and physical inventory counts.

faq.question: Why do auditors care about internal controls?
faq.answer: If internal controls are effective, auditors can rely on them and perform less detailed testing of individual transactions. Weak controls mean more errors could slip through, requiring auditors to test more transactions directly. Control evaluation directly shapes the scope and cost of the audit.
